column3: Immediate preceding speech by the same believer, addressing his people and warning them before the call to follow him.
Pairs steadfastness with refusing the path of the ignorant, reinforcing discernment between competing routes.
Following a guide in order to receive sound judgment closely joins following with rushd.
Pharaoh's claim to guide to the way of rushd is the direct verbal and narrative foil answered by the focus.
Rescue to blessed land suggests a favorable destination but lacks the focus's call to follow and guide.
Denial after clear evidence blocks divine guidance, a general consequence rather than a parallel call.
A messenger addresses his people and directs believers toward reliance on God.
People follow Pharaoh's command, explicitly judged not rashid; it sharply contrasts the focus's offered guidance.
Peace is assigned to those who follow guidance, supporting the focus's association of following with a right course.
It condemns obstructing believers from God's path and seeking to make that path crooked.
A caller identifies his path and those who follow him, grounding allegiance in insight.
Hearing guidance to rushd leads directly to belief, closely matching the focus's promised way of right judgment.
Following the messenger is presented as the means by which people may be guided.
Pharaoh leads his people forward to the Fire, providing the adverse outcome of following his leadership.
Generic description of revelation as guidance and good news for believers.
Contrasts faith and striving in God's way with wrongdoing that does not receive guidance.
People follow a caller on a route with no deviation, echoing ordered following without the rushd claim.
Prophetic and scriptural inheritance yields both guided and rebellious people, without a direct following relation.
Knowledgeable believers commend enduring faith and good work rather than a route of guidance.
Abraham is given his rushd, a concise thematic parallel to the focus's way of rushd.
Following divine approval is contrasted with a destination of wrath, making following consequential.
Immediate earlier speech from the same believing courtier establishes his faith, warning, and the limits of guiding a liar.
Faith is attributed to God's guidance rather than human self-credit, qualifying any human call to guidance.
God does not guide the defiantly rebellious, a general negative counterpart.
A messenger addresses his people without seeking payment, but the verse does not develop guidance or following.
The misled have no path of escape, an indirect consequence of losing guidance.
Unmixed faith brings security and being guided, without a call or route.
It rebukes those who turn believers from God's path and try to make it crooked.
Divinely appointed leaders guide by God's command and embody that guidance in worship and good deeds.
Near-exact formula: a knowledgeable caller says, follow me and I will guide you to a straight path.
Moses commands reform and forbids following the path of corrupters, a clear route-choice parallel.
The unjust follow luxury while a small rescuable group resists corruption, contrasting rival allegiances.
It asks who truly deserves to be followed: the one who guides to truth or one needing guidance.
Its legal warning about usury and repentance does not establish a meaningful guidance or following parallel.
A statement about a prior assumption that humans and jinn would not lie about God.
Clear signs and God's guidance express a broad theological premise, not the focus's interpersonal call.
The messenger disclaims possession of harm or rushd, distinguishing proclamation from control over outcomes.
Divine rescue from distress is relevant only at the broad level of deliverance.
The Quran guides to what is most upright, directly strengthening the focus's orientation toward right conduct.
A man urgently addresses his people with an imperative to follow the messengers, closely paralleling the focus's call.
The misled seek a path of return after punishment, an indirect loss-of-guidance image.
A genuinely more-guiding book is offered as the proper object of following.
The arrogant reject what others believe, but no route or guidance relation is developed.
A self-interested request to follow a departing group is not guidance-oriented allegiance.
Those who follow divine approval are guided through ways of peace and to a straight path.
Pharaoh's threat against alternative worship illuminates the coercive setting in which the believing courtier speaks.
The contrast between possible evil and a Lord-intended rushd is too general for a direct connection.
Faithful worshippers may be among the guided, without the focus's call-and-follow structure.
Harun addresses his people, exposes their trial, and says follow me and obey my command.
Supplication for rescue from darknesses does not itself frame a guided path.
Wrongdoers follow their desires without knowledge, opposed to the focus's offered way of sound judgment.
A question to the messengers about their mission has no substantive route or guidance connection.
Wisdom and decisive speech may support sound judgment, but no following or guidance relation appears.
The speakers hope to be guided after clarification, a remote epistemic parallel.
Opponents reject faith because socially disdained people follow the messenger, exposing resistance to his leadership.
Obedience to a future summons is rewarded, but the military context is not a guidance claim.
The crowd proposes following magicians only if they prevail, a rival and outcome-conditioned allegiance in Pharaoh's setting.
A question to the messengers about their mission has no substantive route or guidance connection.
A ruler must judge by truth and not follow desire lest it lead him away from God's path.
Failure to follow Moses is framed as possible disobedience, making following accountable to a command.
Following a means or course in travel lacks the focus's guidance and moral direction.
Faith is made beloved and its adherents are named the rightly guided, connecting belief with rushd.
God distinguishes those astray from His path and those guided, though without an interpersonal call.
A repeated travel formula about following a means, with no moral guidance claim.
Those who submit are described as seeking rushd, linking submission to the deliberate pursuit of right judgment.
Moses trusts that his Lord will guide him at a moment when the way forward is not visible.
A confused person is called back to guidance after divine guidance, while the verse affirms God's guidance as decisive.
Revelation is described generally as insight, guidance, and mercy for the certain.
Disbelievers issue a false invitation, follow our path, directly contrasting trustworthy and deceptive calls to follow.
Following the recitation concerns reception of revelation rather than following a human guide to rushd.
The arrogant see the way of rushd yet refuse it and instead take the way of error.
Responding to God and believing in Him is linked to becoming rightly directed.
A messenger reports that he conveyed and advised his people after their rejection, without a route formulation.
Failure to answer the call is identified as following desire without guidance from God.
A human question about the earth's upheaval has no meaningful relation to guidance or following.
The Book and criterion are given so that the people may be guided, a broad source-of-guidance parallel.
A messenger reports conveying and advising a people who dislike advisers, without a following claim.
The Creator is stated to be the one who guides the speaker, grounding guidance in God.
A remembered interpreter offers information; the verse does not concern following or right guidance.
The word for following describes harm after charity, not allegiance or a guided route.
Authorized correct speech on the final day only loosely relates to sound judgment.
The Creator is named as the one who will guide, identifying the ultimate source behind guidance.
It forbids following the desires of people who went astray and led many away from the straight path.
Following a teacher is conditioned by patient restraint, but the focus is a different guidance setting.
A disbeliever's claim about future wealth and children has no material route or guidance link.
Obedience to God and the messenger is explicitly said to result in guidance, while the messenger's role is clear delivery.
The verse identifies a persistent physical road, not a moral or guided path.
Shared belief is said to constitute guidance, but no invitation to follow a guide is present.
A conditional claim to follow in battle exposes hypocrisy rather than a route toward right judgment.
It contrasts obedience to a heedless desire-follower with staying among those who call on God.
Hypocrites use oaths to turn people away from God's path, opposing the focus's invitation toward it.
The eventual test distinguishes the companions of the straight path from those who have been guided.
It warns believers against disloyal alliances and names deviation from the straight path, but not a guiding call.
Noah describes disobedience as following people whose wealth and children increase only loss.
Mistreatment of an orphan has no substantive guidance or following relation.
God is sufficient as guide and helper amid prophetic opposition, a general support for divine guidance.
Forgiveness and recompense for deeds do not form a meaningful route or guidance parallel.
The Book is made guidance for Israel and redirects reliance away from other protectors.
The detailed debt-writing regulation does not meaningfully connect to the focus's leadership and guidance claim.
God increases those already guided in guidance, presenting right direction as an ongoing divine gift.
Whoever follows God's guidance is promised freedom from fear and grief, directly linking following to a secure course.
God guides believers through their disputes to the straight path, grounding right direction in divine guidance.
Choosing a way other than that of the believers after guidance has become clear makes following a consequential route-choice.
The Prophet is commanded to follow the guidance of prior prophets, explicitly joining authoritative guidance and following.
God's straight path is to be followed rather than competing ways that divide people from it.
The community is commanded to follow what was sent down from its Lord and not alternative protectors.
God both calls to the abode of peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path.
God identifies the straight way as His, while other paths deviate from it.
The speaker asks for guidance to what is nearer to rushd, directly sharing the focus's key term.
Worship of the one Lord and obedience to the messenger are identified as a straight path.
Later generations neglect prayer and follow desire, with ghayy as the opposed outcome to rushd.
The Creator gives each thing its form and then guides it, identifying God as the source of direction.
Following divine guidance is explicitly contrasted with going astray or falling into misery.
The messenger is said to call his audience to a straight path, closely matching the focus's public guidance claim.
Clear signs are sent down and God guides whom He wills to a straight path.
The willing person is invited to take a way to his Lord, a related formulation of chosen direction.
Human affection cannot control guidance; God alone knows those receptive to it.
Those who strive for God are promised guidance to His ways, extending guidance into sustained action.
One must follow the path of the person who turns repentantly to God, an explicit model of rightly directed allegiance.
Followers blame their leaders for leading them astray, supplying the adverse side of the focus's leadership claim.
Revealed truth is described as guiding to the path of the Mighty and Praiseworthy.
The immediate continuation of 36:20 tells the people to follow messengers who ask no payment and are rightly guided.
God guided Moses and Aaron to the straight path, a concise prophetic precedent for divine direction.
Those who turn to God and follow the best of what they hear are explicitly called the guided.
Listening carefully and following the best message marks those whom God has guided.
The audience is commanded to follow the best of what their Lord has sent down before punishment arrives.
Immediately before the focus, Pharaoh's deceptive ascent project exposes the rival leadership and false assessment the believer answers.
The same believer immediately continues his address by reordering the people's sense of worldly and final destination.
The same speaker contrasts his call to salvation with their call that leads him toward the Fire.
The believer rejects their invitation to disbelief and affirms his call to the Mighty Forgiver.
He concludes that their invitation has no true summons in this world or the next, reinforcing the contrast of calls.
The messenger is said to guide by revelation to a straight path.
Holding fast to revelation is tied directly to being on a straight path.
Jesus commands worship of God and obedience to him, identifying that allegiance as a straight path.
The Prophet is placed on a way of command and told to follow it rather than the desires of the ignorant.
The revealed Book guides to the truth and to a straight path.
God increases those who accept guidance in guidance and grants them their taqwa.
Clear signs are sent down to bring believers from darknesses into light, a related movement of divine direction.
Humanity is shown the way, leaving a response of gratitude or denial.
God finds the Prophet seeking direction and guides him, a direct divine-guidance formulation.
